newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan party denies ready to fund Clinton campaign.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan party denies ready to fund Clinton campaign.

text.p: Taiwan's ruling Nationalist Party on Tuesday denied it was willing to make a huge contribution to U.S. President Bill Clinton's re-election campaign but local media said such largesse would be shrewd politics.

The Chinese-language edition of Asiaweek magazine quoted Liu Tai-ying, chairman of the Nationalist Party's business management committee, as expressing a willingness to donate US$15 million to the Clinton re-election campaign.
"We categorically deny it," party secretary-general Wu Poh-hsiung said in response to the Asiaweek report.
"There is no such thing," Wu told state-funded television. "I spoke to Liu and he told me the report was not true."
Taiwan media quoted Liu as vowing to sue the Hong Kong-based weekly magazine over the report in its latest edition. Wu would not comment and Liu could not be reached.
Whether the Nationalists made a donation or not, local media appeared supportive that such payments were an affordable price of access for politically isolated Taiwan.
"Want to play golf with U.S. President Clinton? Want to be an invited guest at the Democratic Convention?" the United Evening News said in a signed commentary.

"In the diplomatic battlefield, you must buy a ticket," the commentator wrote, saying foreign political parties had to dole out "tangible and intangible" support to gain access to the Democratic Party.

The Democratic National Committee is under fire in the run-up to the November 5 election for accepting hundreds of thousands of dollars in questionable campaign contributions from individuals with ties to the Lippo Group, an Indonesian real estate and banking conglomerate.

Taiwan's Nationalist Party, which ruled China until its civil war defeat in 1949 and flight into exile on the island, is one of the world's richest political organisations with T$37.8 billion (US$1.4 billion) in assets under seven holding firms.
In 1995, party-controlled businesses had combined pretax profits of T$8.6 billion (US$313 million).

The U.S. magazine Newsweek reported this week that a Clinton appointee in Taipei had tried to tap Taiwan's deep political coffers, quoting senior Taiwan officials as saying local firms complained of being pressured to contribute to the campaign.

It said James Wood, chairman of Washington's de facto Taipei embassy, the American Institute in Taiwan, told local executives that Clinton deserved to be rewarded for granting a U.S. visa to Taiwan President Lee Teng-Hui in mid-1995 and for suffering an ensuing firestorm of indignation from China.
Wood denied the charge to Newsweek.

Opposition lawmakers scrambled on Tuesday to profit at the ruling party's expense, saying the Nationalists risked hurting Taiwan's reputation, but also made clear that legal campaign contributions had their usefulness.

"Taiwan has a lot of money. But when we make political contributions to the United States, we must consider whether they violate U.S. law," said lawmaker Tsai Ming-hsien of the main opposition Democratic Progressive Party.
Another opposition deputy said: "We should spend our money to garner diplomatic support. But the money should be spent properly."
